items.title: Air Force Inks Deal for 22 More Boeing F-15EX Fighters
items.author: Greg Hadley
items.summary: The Air Force awarded Boeing a $2.38 billion contract for 22 F-15EX Eagle II fighters on Sept. 29, narrowly meeting a deadline to use funds from last summer’s reconciliation bill or face cuts. The deal, Lot 7 of the program,... The post Air Force Inks Deal for 22 More Boeing F-15EX Fighters appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
The Air Force awarded Boeing a $2.38 billion contract for 22 F-15EX Eagle II fighters on Sept. 29, narrowly meeting a deadline to use funds from last summer’s reconciliation bill or face cuts.

The deal, Lot 7 of the program, brings to 120 the total number of F-15EXs under contract. The Air Force had planned to end production at 129 jets, but increased the total program in April to 269 aircraft.

Boeing earned the deal on the same day as the Navy announced it had selected Boeing to build its next-generation air dominance fighter, F/A-XX. The win means Boeing has won both the Air Force’s and Navy’s sixth-generation fighter competitons.

The F-15EX, meanwhile, is a heavily upgraded version of the fourth-generation F-15, leading some to dub it a “4.5 generation” fighter. Its digital fly-by-wire flight controls complement an all-glass touch-screen cockpit, a new APG-82 active electronically scanned array radar, and the Eagle Passive Active Warning Survivability System (EPAWSS), an advanced electronic warfare suite.

Funding for Lot 7 came from $115 million in the 2026 budget and another $2.8 billion in last year’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” reconciliation package. That bill came with a caveat, though: any funds not spent by Oct. 1, 2026, would be reduced by 8.3 percent. The threatened reduction provided the pressure to close the deal before the fiscal year ends Sept. 30.

In a release, the Air Force trumpeted its success in meeting that deadline.

“This award followed extensive collaboration among program management, contracting, pricing, engineering, financial management, logistics and other acquisition professionals,” the release states. “The team assessed the impacts of changing production conditions and inflation, aligned the aircraft procurement with available funding, and completed the action before the fiscal-year deadline.”

At $2.38 billion for 22 jets, the average cost works out to $108 million, which does not include engines from GE Aerospace, which the Air Force purchases separately.

Boeing said in a release that it is currently delivering Lot 3 aircraft and will continue to do so for the rest of the year. Boeing is working with the Pentagon to up its production to two F-15EXs per month.

The F-15EX contract was not Boeing’s only win Sept. 29–the Navy also announced it had selected the firm to build its new sixth-generation F/A-XX fighter.

items.body: FORT BRAGG, N.C. – When collegiate wrestling athletes meet Army special operations at the U.S. Army John F. Kennedy Special Warfare Center and School, the common ground is forged in sweat, performance, and the pursuit of excellence. The Special Operations Center of Excellence welcomed 39 members from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill’s wrestling team to experience holistic methods to physical training, cognitive exercises, virtual reality exercises, and nutrition Q & A sessions at the Human Performance Force Generation Training Center, commonly referred to as HP FORGE, at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, Sept. 21, 2026. While physical training and mental grit paralleled both institutions for preparation on the mat and in the tactical training environment, the visit embodied attributes that would inspire future force generation. “Taking our team to the Special Warfare Center and School at Fort Bragg was eye opening,” said Rob Koll, the head wrestling coach at UNC Chapel Hill. “A lot of our young athletes don’t necessarily appreciate the size and scope of the training and expertise that goes into preparing our special operations Soldiers. This put our guys through a small taste of it.” By showcasing the state-of-the-art training center, the Special Operations Center of Excellence put the Department of War’s warrior readiness and human performance initiatives on display. The visit highlighted how both institutions utilize sports science, mental resilience, and advanced nutrition. “Seeing the science behind the methods, how carefully everything is structured for performance, recovery, and resilience, gave our team a whole new level of respect for the process,” Koll said. Beyond tactical training, the engagement served as a pillar in the U.S. Army John F. Kennedy Special Warfare Center and School by informing and building trust with the American people. “The visit doesn’t just provide a tour of what we do here, but it shows the first SOF truth that people are more important than hardware,” said Michael Fields, Human Performance and Wellness deputy director. “We do that in a few ways by demonstrating metric-driven recovery and prevention methods, such as physical therapy, mental health, cognitive performance, and physical training. It’s a one-stop holistic shop for training, performance, and rehabilitation.” During their visit, the wrestling team divided into three groups to experience a three-station rotation. Each station focused on a unique area: a 30-minute workout led by a performance coach, classroom discussion on nutrition led by a dietitian, and a virtual reality shooting demo highlighting cognitive precision. For the wrestling team, the visit not only demonstrated an intersection between Army special operations and human performance with collegiate athletes, but the physical training session served as a solemn tribute to a fallen teammate from the Human Performance and Wellness staff lost in 2025. Named in memory of Nick Vetell, the team completed a conditioning session built from the final training program he crafted. “We remember and celebrate Nick in many ways,” said Jamie Hiegel, the HPW strength and conditioning coach at HP FORGE, who led the workout during the visit. “Having UNC wrestling visit us and participate in the last workout Nick did before his passing allowed all of us another opportunity to remember and celebrate him. We thank him for that.” Before Vetell joined HPW at the Special Warfare Center and School, he served as the assistant strength and conditioning coach at UNC Chapel Hill. “He was a very driven human,” said Luke Simcox, a UNC wrestler and a junior studying exercise and sports science. “He provided so many resources for us. […] Just knowing that he was here and the type of person he was and his goals felt like an extra connection to him. It’s kind of like his legacy still lives on.” Following their time at the HP FORGE and lunch at the Sgt. Gordon D. Yntema Dining Facility, the wrestling team stepped back in time at the JFK Special Warfare Museum, where they learned about the history of special warfare from various exhibits and museum curators. “We had the opportunity to visit the museum, which reminded us of the courage, sacrifice, and the elite standards of those who defend our freedom,” Koll said. “I’m truly grateful for the opportunity and for the professionals, who shared their knowledge with us.” For Simcox, who has been wrestling for 18 years, he received the experience with an open mind. Between training and preparing for wrestling meets, he sees similarities in training that encompass not just a physical component to preparation but a mental one. “Wrestling is a very mental sport, which may be the same thing that Soldiers go through,” Simcox said. “I think a lot of wrestlers feel a connection to some of these Soldiers. You see some wrestlers come into the Army or Special Forces after their collegiate experiences. Being around these guys who are here and dedicated to serving our country is a very surreal experience.” The experience served as a moment of reflection for Simcox, whose respect for the armed forces is rooted at home. Coming from a family of military service spanning the naval, marine, and aviation branches, the UNC wrestler noted that walking through the Special Warfare Center and School felt like a glimpse into a potential future. “I had a family member in the Marines, one that was an engineer in the Navy, and one that was in the Air Force,” he said. “I might have to be the one to be in the Army; it is very intriguing. I have a very open mind and will see where it takes me. I would love to serve our country.”

items.title: From Excess to Readiness: I Corps Tackles ARSTRUC Equipment Challenge
items.author: CPT Francesca Hamilton
items.summary: 593rd Corps Sustainment Command, I Corps established and continues to manage a CL VII yard at Joint Base Lewis-McChord in order to manage the broken and excess equipment surplus from the ARSTRUC realignment.
items.body: The 2025 Army Transformation Initiative and ARSTRUC effort continue to reshape force design, realign capabilities, and eliminate outdated authorizations across the Army. These reforms aim to streamline the Army by reducing waste, modernizing acquisition, and restructuring units for future combat requirements. Over the past year, units across Joint Base Lewis-McChord faced an overwhelming surge in excess and broken equipment requiring disposition. The restructure left commanders with rapidly changing property-book requirements and few outlets to divest legacy or no-longer‑authorized items. The result was a growing backlog of equipment that units could neither store nor repair, intensifying the need for a streamlined, accountable turn‑in process at installation level. With Modernization Displacement and Repair Site (MDRS) no longer available, and Equipment Redistribution Divestiture Site (ERDS) operations concluded, a new installation-level solution had to be developed. I Corps established a standardized Class VII turn‑in process at JBLM by partnering with the 593rd Corps Sustainment Command’s Supply Support Activity (SSA). This initiative began immediately following the conclusion of the Army Sustainment Command’s ERDS operations in January 2026, and JBLM units were able to utilize the 593rd Class VII yard in February 2026. This partnership, operated and supervised by the 13th Combat Sustainment Support Battalion, responds directly to the loss of the MDRS in May 2025. This closure eliminated one of the Army’s most effective avenues for large‑scale equipment divestiture, leaving units with limited options and creating potential property-book backlogs, storage constraints, and delays to modernization efforts. Chief Warrant Officer 2 Gilberto Pimentel explained, “The JBLM Class VII Yard was created to help units maintain momentum in their divestment efforts following the conclusion of MDRS and ERDS cycles, providing a streamlined path to offload excess equipment. What began as a rapid response grew into a reliable capability that supports readiness, accountability, and the Army’s ongoing transformation under ARSTRUC.” Under the new installation-level model, units coordinate scheduled turn‑in appointments with the 13th CSSB‑operated Class VII Turn‑In Yard. This controlled process enables the SSA to assume accountability of equipment using DD Form 1348 or DA Form 2062. The formal transfer provides commanders immediate relief from the daily burden of managing excess equipment while maintaining a clearly documented accountability trail. The 13th CSSB supports yard operations with dedicated material-handling capability, including wreckers, Palletized Load System trucks, and forklifts. These resources ensure equipment is safely recovered, transported, staged, and protected as it moves through the disposition pipeline. SSA personnel, integrated into the yard’s operating rhythm through the 593rd CSC Multiclass Section, validate each item’s National Item Identification Number, quantity, condition code, and supporting documentation. After verification, the SSA processes the equipment in GCSS‑Army and produces the required turn‑in documentation under the SSA Routing Identifier Code. This transfers accountability from the losing unit’s property book into SSA‑managed stock, enabling redistribution, reissue, or further disposition. Staff Sgt. Jose Mart Raquino highlighted the importance of this relationship, noting that, “Partnering with the 593rd CSC’s SSA allows commanders to divest excess Class VII the right way: accountability transfers on documented, verified terms, so units get immediate property-book relief without ever losing audit-readiness.” To preserve SSA capacity, items directed to Defense Logistics Agency Disposition Services are sent directly to DLA rather than retained at the Class VII yard. This keeps the yard focused on equipment with continuing Army value and prevents long‑term storage challenges. For commanders across JBLM, the benefits are immediate: reduced property-book complexity, fewer inventory discrepancies, more focus on mission-essential equipment, and increased space for modernization and fielding. The model reinforces the I Corps commander’s intent to maintain property accountability at the appropriate command level while supporting readiness across the formation. The JBLM Class VII Turn‑In Yard demonstrates a practical command–sustainment partnership. Units receive an accountable and predictable path to divest excess equipment, while sustainment organizations maintain the visibility and control required to route Army assets to their proper disposition. By standardizing turn‑in procedures, I Corps is improving property accountability, preserving resources, and allowing commanders to focus on the equipment required for future operations. All units on JBLM are authorized to use the site. So far, it has been utilized by three brigades, seven Direct Reporting Units across JBLM, USAAD Yakima, and 54 different companies within those organizations. As Sgt. Kenneth Juarez from the 24th Composite Supply Company described, “Being a 92A in the 24th CSC SSA can be challenging, but knowing that I am helping the units of I Corps with their mission readiness inspires me to be the most proficient logistics specialist I can be.”

items.title: Why the Pentagon just dropped $450M on tungsten mining
items.author: Daniel Terrill
items.summary: The Pentagon recently announced a $450 million investment in The Elmet Group to strengthen the U.S. supply chain for the critical mineral tungsten.
items.body:
The Defense Department announced this month a $450 million investment in The Elmet Group to strengthen the U.S. supply chain for tungsten, a critical mineral used for manufacturing military weapons ranging from bullets to missiles.

The investment comes as a federal procurement rule barring tungsten mined, refined, or processed in China, Russia, Iran and North Korea from defense applications nears its Jan. 1 deadline.

In the announcement, the Defense Department said it chose to invest in Elmet because it is “the only U.S.-owned, fully integrated producer of tungsten and molybdenum materials and components.”

“This investment reflects the Department’s commitment to rebuilding critical industrial capacity in the United States,” said Michael Cadenazzi, the Defense Department’s assistant secretary for industrial base policy.

He added that it will “strengthen supply chain resilience, support high-quality manufacturing jobs, and reinforce the production base behind essential defense systems.”

Chris Berry, a critical-minerals analyst, explained on his podcast that China dominates the global tungsten supply chain, while the U.S. has not mined tungsten since 2015.

Although ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have increased pressure on tungsten demand, Berry argued that its rising price is “due almost exclusively to policy choices in Beijing and Washington.”

“The free flow of tungsten material is for now a thing of the past,” he said, adding that those policies have created “two distinct markets” and driven a rapid increase in prices.

According to government data, China controls about 85% of the world’s tungsten supply and 40% of its molybdenum, a similar material that is often mined in the same areas.

While tungsten is primarily used to make tools for manufacturing, Berry said the metal is also used for fabricating semiconductors for AI data centers and he called it “a must-have” for the defense industry because of its unique properties.

Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal and is roughly as dense as gold. When combined with carbon, it forms tungsten carbide, an extremely hard material used in industrial and military applications.

“There’s no good substitute at scale for most of these applications,” Berry said, describing tungsten demand as relatively small in absolute terms but highly resistant to price changes.

However, mining more tungsten is only part of the challenge, Berry said. The country also needs the ability to refine and process the metal into usable materials.

“Every mined dollar should be paired with a processing dollar,” he said, adding that other potential remedies include price protection, defense stockpiling and greater reliance on allied suppliers to spread supply-chain risk.

According to the announcement, the company supports more than 100 defense programs, including Patriot, Javelin, AEGIS, Trident II and THAAD, as well as Virginia- and Columbia-class submarines.

Elmet, based in Portland, Maine, was founded privately in 1929 but went public earlier this year. It will use $165 million of the funds to upgrade domestic manufacturing operations in Maine, Michigan and Ohio to increase productivity.

The company said in a press release that it will put approximately $150 million toward restarting tungsten mining operations in Imlay, Nevada; and another $100 million for establishing a refining and trading division to support access and international partnerships.

Since the agreement, Elmet said it has secured agreements for mining operations with Tungsten West in England and the Vietnam-based Masan High-Tech Materials Corporation.

Daniel Terrill is a contributor to Military Times. He’s been reporting on military issues, the gun industry, and the outdoors for nearly two decades. Although writing is his passion, he’s been a Marine, police officer, and, perhaps the most dangerous job of his career, a substitute teacher.

items.title: Hegseth to Slash 20 Percent of Generals and Flag Officers, Deepening Cuts to Senior Officers
items.author: Chris Gordon
items.summary: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth plans to announce Sept. 30 that the Pentagon will slash the number of general and flag officers by 20 percent The post Hegseth to Slash 20 Percent of Generals and Flag Officers, Deepening Cuts to Senior Officers appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth plans to announce Sept. 30 a directive to slash the number of general and flag officers across the U.S. military by 20 percent, Pentagon officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

Hegseth is doubling down on the 10 percent cut to general and flag officers he ordered last year, which he dubbed the “less generals, more GIs” policy.

Hegseth’s announcement will come during a “State for the Force” address. The cuts will reduce the number of general and flag officer billets, meaning some moves may play out over time, rather than swiftly removing 20 percent of generals and admirals.

Fox News first reported the new cuts and details of the planned announcement. Pentagon officials later confirmed that account.

The “State of the Force” speech comes a year after Hegseth convened senior U.S. military leaders from commands around the globe to outline his philosophy for running the Pentagon—an extraordinarily rare gathering.

The services are expected to make the cuts by Jan. 1, 2027. How reductions will be apportioned among the services is, so far, unclear.

Generals and admirals make up less than 1 percent of the military. According to the Congressional Research Service data, there were about 850 general officer positions in 2023. Some of those positions were unfilled at the time, as is the case today.

The maximum number of general officers allowed per service is set by law, though those caps do not apply to joint positions. The law also sets a minimum number of general officers in joint jobs.

The Air Force has roughly 250 generals. The Space Force has roughly 30 generals, and had plans to continue to grow that number.

In Hegseth’s Quantico address a year ago, he told the ranking military officers and senior enlisted advisers in the audience that “more leadership changes will be made” and asserted that “fat generals and admirals” were roaming the halls of the Pentagon.

A top Democratic lawmaker complained the cuts were arbitrary and Congress had not been consulted, and noted that Hegseth has removed senior officers from their roles without explanation.

“Efficiency and streamlining in the military are worthy goals, but the size and structure of our military’s senior officer corps are matters in which Congress has a fundamental role,” said Sen. Jack Reed (D-R.I.), the ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee. “Article I of the Constitution assigns Congress the power to raise and support the armed forces and to make rules for their government. Reshaping the senior leadership of the world’s most powerful military is precisely the kind of decision that requires consultation with and justification to Congress.”

The new cuts are not the only step Hegseth is taking this week to reshape the military establishment. In a Sept. 29 memo released by the Pentagon, Hegseth directed military service academies to drop tenured positions for civilian professors. Hegseth said the move was needed because “civilian academic norms … dilute our focus on lethality.”

Critics have said the Pentagon’s efforts to reform the institutions could compromise the academic independence and the quality of education at the service academies, which include the U.S. Air Force Academy, the U.S. Naval Academy, and the U.S. Military Academy at West Point.

USAFA only recently began offering tenure to civilian faculty.

Hegseth served in the Army National Guard as a major and has cast himself as a Pentagon chief who relates to rank-and-file troops.

His previous directive to reduce general officers mandated a 20 percent reduction in Active four-stars, a 20 percent cut in National Guard generals, and a 10 percent cut in overall general and flag officers. Hegseth has said that cuts were needed to reduce bureaucracy.

items.title: Zero Discrepancies. Zero Exceptions. Flawless Execution at NAVSUP FLC Pearl Harbor
items.author: Wesley Burgos
items.summary: Naval Supply Systems Command (NAVSUP) Fleet Logistics Center (FLC) Pearl Harbor personnel supported a flawless Navy Working Capital Fund (NWCF) inventory audit conducted by Ernst & Young at Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard (PHNSY) and Intermediate Maintenance Facility and Marine Aviation Logistics Squadron 24 (MALS24) from Sept. 21-24, 2026. The audit covered more than $220 million in financial value and found no discrepancies or exceptions.
items.body:
PEARL HARBOR, Hawaii — Naval Supply Systems Command (NAVSUP) Fleet Logistics Center (FLC) Pearl Harbor personnel supported a flawless Navy Working Capital Fund (NWCF) inventory audit conducted by Ernst & Young at Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard (PHNSY) and Intermediate Maintenance Facility and Marine Aviation Logistics Squadron 24 (MALS24) from Sept. 21-24, 2026. The audit covered more than $220 million in financial value and found no discrepancies or exceptions.

The evaluation examined more than 100 National Item Identification Numbers (NIINs) and hundreds of individual items for existence and completeness, providing a direct measure of the systems and controls used to account for mission essential resources.

“There is no margin for error when the fleet depends on us,” said Capt. Anthony Bannister, commanding officer, NAVSUP Fleet Logistics Center Pearl Harbor. “These audit results exemplify the standard we expect at NAVSUP FLC Pearl Harbor: precision in execution, accountability for every resource and an unwavering focus on delivering what the fleet needs, when it needs it.”

Cyril “Cy” Yuvienco, NAVSUP Fleet Logistics Center Pearl Harbor Regional Inventory Accuracy Officer (RIAO), said the result demonstrates the command’s ability to maintain data integrity and ensure physical inventory aligns with digital records.

“Achieving zero discrepancies and zero exceptions during the EY audit demonstrates that NAVSUP FLC Pearl Harbor delivers flawless data integrity, proving its physical inventory matches digital ledgers and validating that command internal controls are ironclad,” said Yuvienco. “This absolute precision maximizes fleet readiness by eliminating logistical delays, ensuring critical parts are exactly where they should be.”

That result was built before auditors arrived. FLC Pearl Harbor RIAO personnel worked with plant personnel to conduct location surveys, pre inventory checks and dry runs of the live walkthroughs while resolving administrative challenges ahead of the evaluation.

“Behind the scenes, the audit’s success hinged on relentless cross command synchronization and collaboration with plant personnel,” said Yuvienco. “This meticulous preparation ensured a rapid response network that could instantly satisfy auditor data requests.”

During the live inventory demonstration, auditors observed physical verification, material staging and digital documentation in real time.

The audit brought together personnel from NAVSUP, Naval Sea Systems Command (NAVSEA), the RIAO, plant personnel, MALS 24 and supporting organizations to provide the access, documentation and resources required for the evaluation.

For NAVSUP Fleet Logistics Center Pearl Harbor, the result reinforces a simple standard: when the fleet depends on the logistics enterprise, the details must be right.

At NAVSUP Fleet Logistics Center Pearl Harbor, readiness starts with relationships. Precision, accountability and execution forge those relationships into readiness, while service is delivered with aloha.

As one of 11 commands within the NAVSUP Enterprise, NAVSUP Fleet Logistics Center Pearl Harbor enables forward operations and sustains fleet readiness throughout the Indo-Pacific. Naval Supply Systems Command provides supply, acquisition and logistics support to the Navy and joint force worldwide. Headquartered in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania, NAVSUP employs military and civilian personnel across the globe. Together, NAVSUP and the Navy Supply Corps conduct and enable global supply chain management, acquisition, operational logistics, and Sailor and family services in partnership with the fleet to generate readiness and sustain naval forces.

items.title: Ready When it Matters: Hawaiʻi National Guard Helps Neighbors During Hurricane Nolo
items.author: Rachel Blaire
items.summary: When flooding made communities unsafe during Hurricane Nolo, Hawaiʻi National Guard (HING) soldiers with Task Force Hawaiʻi were ready to move. On the night of Sept. 26, Task Force Hawaiʻi conducted five high-water rescue missions on Hawaiʻi Island, rescuing 19 civilians from flood-affected areas and transporting them to a shelter in Nāʻālehu.
items.body:
When flooding made communities unsafe during Hurricane Nolo, Hawaiʻi National Guard (HING) soldiers with Task Force Hawaiʻi were ready to move.

On the night of Sept. 26, Task Force Hawaiʻi conducted five high-water rescue missions on Hawaiʻi Island, rescuing 19 civilians from flood-affected areas and transporting them to a shelter in Nāʻālehu.

“We had been preparing for this storm for a while so when we got the call, we were ready to respond immediately,” said Sgt. Kanaʻi Coyaso, Task Force Hawaiʻi.

The missions were part of a statewide HING response that placed more than 450 soldiers and airmen across Hawaiʻi ahead of Hurricane Nolo. On Hawaiʻi Island, approximately 120 Guard members assigned to Task Force Hawaiʻi were positioned to support Hawaiʻi County, with six High-Water Vehicle Teams staged around the county for quick response.

During one mission, Coyaso and other soldiers reached a civilian on foot and escorted the person from their home to the back of a high-water vehicle.

“In that moment, you’re not thinking about anything else you’re focused on getting that person out,” Coyaso said. “Once we reached them, our priority was making sure everyone made it back to safety.”

The rescue teams were operating in conditions that included flooding and high winds as Hurricane Nolo moved through the islands. Although Nolo did not make landfall in Hawaiʻi, the storm still produced hazardous conditions and flooding that prompted requests for assistance from county authorities.

For Spc. Marc Lee Tagalicud of Task Force Hawaiʻi, one of those missions became a reminder of why the Guard is “Always Ready and Always There.”

“We rescued two civilians who had family members across the road, but the flooding made it dangerous for them to cross,” Tagalicud said. “We used a high-water vehicle to get them safely across, then walked them to their family.”

Tagalicud then gave the older man his own wet weather top to help keep him dry.

“It felt good to be able to help a member of our community,” he said.

The High-Water Vehicle Teams are trained to operate in flooded areas where conventional vehicles may not be able to safely travel and are deployed under the direction of civil authorities for life-safety and emergency response missions.

“Our Guardsmen are integrated with the Hawaii County Civil Defense Agency, and we had our vehicles staged in strategic positions around the island,” said Hawai‘i Task Force Commander Maj. Keoki Leong. “Though Hurricane Nolo did not make landfall, some flooding and high winds still impacted Hawai‘i County causing damage and that kept us ‘at the ready’ supporting throughout the night.”

For Leong, the response was another example of the importance of being ready before the emergency arrives. “I am proud of our readiness for Hurricane Nolo and the Guard's support to our County when they need it,” he said.

The HING also positioned personnel and High-Water Vehicle Teams on Oʻahu, Maui and Kauaʻi in coordination with state and county emergency management agencies, fire and police departments, and other state and federal partners.

“This is exactly why we posture our personnel and equipment before a storm arrives,” said the Hawaiʻi Adjutant General Maj. Gen. Stephen Logan. “Our Soldiers and Airmen were ready to move when the call came, and they were quickly able to help get people out of dangerous conditions and to a safe location.”

The Nolo response builds on the Guard’s experience supporting communities during Hurricane Lala and Hurricane Lowell and also before the storms.

“We don't wait for the emergency to happen before we begin preparing,” Logan said. “The relationships and communication that we have with the mayors and county emergency managers during 'blue skies' are important. It allows us to anticipate needs and execute exercised plans.”

Hurricane Nolo was the fourth storm since the beginning of August to threaten the Hawaiian Islands, each bringing the potential for flooding, high winds and other hazards to communities across Hawaiʻi.

Through each storm, HING soldiers and airmen have remained ready to answer the call, preparing personnel and equipment before they are needed and responding when communities request assistance.

items.title: Capsized yola-type vessel calls for multi-agency rescue
items.author: Ozzy Trevino

items.title: US Navy selects Boeing to build next-generation F/A-XX fighter
items.author: Claire Barrett, J.D. Simkins
items.summary: Boeing has officially been selected to build the Navy’s sixth-generation carrier-based strike fighter, dubbed F/A-XX.
items.body:
Boeing has been selected to build the Navy’s sixth-generation carrier-based strike fighter, dubbed F/A-XX, icing out what was considered to be its biggest competitor in late-stage negotiations, Northrop Grumman.

Inked at $20 billion for the full-scale development phase, the contract, according to a Pentagon release, “procures multiple test aircraft for ground, airworthiness, systems, and weapons integration testing.”

“The F/A-XX is a critical pillar in our commitment to maintaining peace through strength,” Michael P. Duffey, under secretary of defense for Acquisition and Sustainment, said in the release. “F/A-XX will dominate contested airspace, extend operational reach, and deliver a decisive combat advantage for the warfighter.”

Equipped with an extended range to provide power projection from U.S. carriers, Boeing has promised that the F/A-XX will, crucially, be interoperable with both manned and unmanned platforms such as Collaborative Combat Aircraft.

“This achievement marks a new era for the U.S. Navy,” said acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao. “The Sixth-Generation fighter is a generational leap in air superiority and will provide the world’s best aviators with unparalleled capabilities to fight, win, and come home safe. We are excited to partner with Boeing, and for our warfighters to continue to dominate the skies and defeat our nation’s enemies.”

Boeing’s contract award marks another milestone victory for the company, which has now all but guaranteed its monopoly on sixth-generation fighters across the services.

In 2025, Boeing beat out Lockheed Martin for the contract to build the U.S. Air Force’s sixth-generation fighter under the Next Generation Air Dominance program, or NGAD.

That aircraft, since dubbed the F-47, has entered its engineering and manufacturing development phase, one service official announced in July, with first flights expected as early as 2028.

The Air Force at the time announced plans to purchase at least 185 of the next-gen fighters, a number designed to replace the F-22 Raptor fleet.

The F/A-XX program, meanwhile, which has yet to receive its official designation, has been the subject of funding disputes for years, with engineering and supply chain concerns prompting some Pentagon officials to push for delaying the program.

The carrier-based fighter jet is slated to anchor the Navy’s next-generation fighter fleet — operating alongside the F-35 — and is expected to replace the aging inventory of F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and EA-18G Growlers beginning in the 2030s.

“It’s an honor to be selected to produce the Navy’s first sixth-generation platform,” Steve Parker, president and chief executive officer of Boeing Defense, Space & Security, said in a release announcing the deal. “Backed by decades of work, bolstered by game-changing innovations and solidified by the investments we’ve made in new facilities uniquely suited to build multiple products with next-generation capabilities, our dedicated and talented team is ready to execute this critical program.”

Claire Barrett is an editor and military history correspondent for Military Times. She holds a master's degree in military history from King's College, London, and is also a World War II researcher with an unparalleled affinity for Sir Winston Churchill and Michigan football.

J.D. Simkins is Editor-in-Chief of Military Times and Defense News, and a Marine Corps veteran of the Iraq War.

items.title: F-47 Maker Boeing Tapped for Navy’s F/A-XX Sixth-Gen Fighter
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: The Navy has awarded Boeing a contract worth more than $20 billion to build its new carrier-based sixth-generation fighter, the F/A-XX. Boeing is also building the Air Force’s sixth-gen F-47. The post F-47 Maker Boeing Tapped for Navy’s F/A-XX Sixth-Gen Fighter appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
The Navy has awarded Boeing a contract worth more than $20 billion to build its new carrier-based sixth-generation fighter, the F/A-XX. Boeing is also building the Air Force’s sixth-gen F-47.

“The F/A-XX is a critical pillar in our commitment to maintaining peace through strength,” Michael P. Duffey, the undersecretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, said in a Sept. 29 release from the Pentagon “F/A-XX will dominate contested airspace, extend operational reach, and deliver a decisive combat advantage for the warfighter. The F/A-XX platform represents a crucial, non-negotiable investment in America’s national security and long-term air combat capabilities.”

The Pentagon release states that the F/A-XX will first augment, and eventually replace, older F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and EA-18G Growlers beginning in the 2030s. It will operate alongside the carrier-based F-35C Joint Strike Fighters, which the Navy and Marine Corps both fly.

The selection ensures Boeing will make two of the three sixth-generation aircraft in development for the U.S. military—the firm won the contract for the Air Force’s sixth-gen fighter program in March 2025 with the F-47. It also represents a loss for Northrop Grumman, the only other company that remained in the running for the Navy’s Next-Generation Air Dominance fighter, and the maker of the Air Force’s B-21 Raider.

“We are joining forces with Boeing to field these capabilities rapidly, ensuring our warfighters possess the lethal and highly networked systems required to deter aggression, project undisputed power, and secure absolute air superiority,” Duffey said.

The Pentagon release said F/A-XX will be able to fly alongside and control semi-autonomous Navy drones known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft.

“This achievement marks a new era for the U.S. Navy,” acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said. “The sixth-generation fighter is a generational leap in air superiority and will provide the world’s best aviators with unparalleled capabilities to fight, win, and come home safe. We are excited to partner with Boeing, and for our warfighters to continue to dominate the skies and defeat our nation’s enemies.”

Advanced stealth is also considered to be a key attribute of sixth-generation aircraft.

Now-retired Rear Adm. Michael Donnelly, the former director of the Navy’s air warfare division, said at an April 2025 conference that F/A-XX could be the Navy’s last manned fighter.

“It could be our last tactical manned fighter that we operate out of the Navy,” Donnelly said at the Navy League’s Sea Air Space conference in National Harbor, Md. “It will actually be at a point where we are more man-on-the-loop than man-in-the-loop, and be the bridge to fully integrating towards the hybrid air wing [combining piloted aircraft and unmanned platforms] in the future, in the 2040s.”

Donnelly told reporters at that conference that F/A-XX would likely be able to fly more than 25 percent farther than current Navy fighters before needing refueling. The F/A-18 Super Hornet has a roughly 1,275-nautical mile combat range, which is slightly more than the F-35C Joint Strike Fighter’s combat range of more than 1,200 nautical miles.

“That’s a core attribute of the F/A-XX,” Donnelly said in 2025. “It will definitely have longer inherent range, and then with refueling, you could say that’s indefinite, as long as refueling is available.”

Boeing said in a statement that F/A-XX “will revolutionize advancements in open mission systems architecture, advanced mission systems, and operational reach and capacity.”

“It’s an honor to be selected to produce the Navy’s first sixth-generation platform,” Steve Parker, president and chief executive officer of Boeing Defense, Space and Security, said in the company’s own statement. “Backed by decades of work, bolstered by game-changing innovations and solidified by the investments we’ve made in new facilities uniquely suited to build multiple products with next-generation capabilities, our dedicated and talented team is ready to execute this critical program.”

Boeing said technical and program details on the F/A-XX are classified and could not be released.

Longtime defense analyst J.J. Gertler said the Navy’s choice of Boeing could leverage work Boeing is now doing with its F-47 sixth-generation fighter for the Air Force. That connection could accelerate the F/A-XX process and get it into production faster.

“If it’s based on the F-47 or was codeveloped with the F-47, they might be able to put an aircraft in the air very quickly,” Gertler told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

Boeing has invested heavily in building more facilities for advanced aircraft production in St. Louis, Mo., where the F-47 is now in the works, Gertler said.

Boeing is also building F-15EX Eagle II fighters and T-7 Red Hawk trainer jets for the Air Force in St. Louis. Indeed, also on Sept. 29, the Pentagon awarded Boeing a $2.38 billion contract for 22 more F-15EX fighters.

Boeing said construction is still ongoing for its secure manufacturing facility in St. Louis, which will “be part of the world’s most advanced, all-digital aerospace design and manufacturing system.”

“Delivering two advanced fighters in parallel was always our plan, and we invested accordingly,” Parker said. “We are ready and able to build multiple concurrent future combat aircraft franchise programs.”

Gertler said it remains to be seen whether Boeing will be able to follow through on commitments for many critical military aircraft.

“We don’t know how much of [Boeing’s new advanced aircraft facility] is taken up by F-47,” Gertler said. “They’ve got F-15EX numbers expanding. They’ve got T-7 there. Do they have the people to be able to produce this [F/A-XX] aircraft quickly?”

REDSTONE ARSENAL, Ala. — The U.S. Army awarded five separate Other Transaction Authority (OTA) agreements on Sept. 29, 2026, to develop prototype systems for the Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) Increment 4. The recipients are Anduril, Castelion, Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control, Mach Industries, and RTX. Under these agreements, each company will develop prototype missiles capable of launching from the M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) and striking moving maritime and relocatable land targets at ranges of 1,000 kilometers or greater. The program follows a phased competition timeline: • Fiscal Year 2027: Initial prototype development will culminate in a competitive fly-off and down-select. • Fiscal Year 2028: Vendors demonstrating mature, successful designs will be eligible for follow-on agreements and a final competitive fly-off.

items.title: Pentagon Hands Out $20.7B Contract for AMRAAM Missiles to RTX
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: The Pentagon on Sept. 28 announced a contract potentially worth $20.7 billion for RTX to build Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles used by Navy and Air Force aircraft and for ground-based interceptors. The post Pentagon Hands Out $20.7B Contract for AMRAAM Missiles to RTX appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
The Pentagon on Sept. 28 announced a contract potentially worth $20.7 billion for RTX to build Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles used by Navy and Air Force aircraft and for ground-based interceptors.

The announcement of the Sept. 25 award noted that the contract is for five years, with two optional years, and is meant to ramp up production of the munition, used for air-to-air combat and missile defense.

The Pentagon release highlights both roles of the AIM-120 AMRAAM as “a proven air-to-air capability” and a “critical air defense capability for U.S. and allied forces.”

In its own release, RTX said the money would “accelerate production of AMRAAM missiles to record-setting levels” but did not specify the quantities.

However, RTX’s Raytheon division previously announced in February it had reached “framework” agreements to boost annual production of the AMRAAM to at least 1,900 missiles annually, along with increased production of the Tomahawk, SM-3 Block IB, SM-3 Block IIA, and SM-6 missiles, all of which are Raytheon products.

The latest contract award does not make clear whether the $20.7 billion is funding for the framework agreement or a separate deal. Neither the Pentagon nor RTX immediately responded to a request for comment.

The Air Force’s fiscal 2026 spending plan included $680 million for 423 AMRAAMs, split between regular appropriations and reconciliation funding.

The new $20.7 billion contract aims to supply the USAF, Navy, and potentially foreign military sales, according to the release.

The AIM-120 is a radar-guided, supersonic missile. According to RTX, 11 currently operational platforms across 40 nations use it, including:

- F-15 Eagle / F-15E Strike Eagle / F-15EX Eagle II

- F-16 Fighting Falcon

- F/A-18 Hornet & F/A-18E/F Super Hornet

- F-22A Raptor

- F-35 Lightning II

- AV-8B Harrier II

- Eurofighter Typhoon

- JAS 39 Gripen

- FA-50 / T-50 Golden Eagle

- NASAMS (National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System)

- SL-AMRAAM / CLAWS Ground Launchers

There are three variants: the “B” model, which offers reprogrammable aspects not on the initial AMRAAM; the “C” model, which has smaller control surfaces so the F-22 and F-35 can carry it and high-angle off-boresight launch capability; and the “D” model with GPS-assisted guidance, improved range, updated data links, and jam resistance.

The latest version, with System Improvement Program update III, was fielded in March 2024.

The Pentagon plans SIP IV and SIP V upgrades, which will increase the munition’s computing power to four times its current level and expand its engagement envelope.

USAF has announced plans to use the AMRAAM alongside its still-under-development AIM-260 Joint Air Tactical Missile.

Air & Space Forces Magazine reported on Sept. 17 that Lockheed Martin announced a deal to expand JATM production through a separate multiyear agreement. Beyond production, the Air Force also faces operational availability problems with another air-to-air missile, the AIM-9X Sidewinder, as Air & Space Forces Magazine recently reported.

Both the AIM-9X and AIM-120 are key for tactical aircraft operations. The Sidewinder is a within-visual-range, dogfighting missile, while the 12.7-foot-long AMRAAM is a “fire-and-forget” missile used for beyond-visual-range interception.

The 9.8-foot-long AIM-9X uses imaging infrared focal plane array seeking technology, while the AMRAAM uses active radar and conducts mid-course updates for terminal strikes. The Sidewinder can strike targets up to 22 miles away, while the AMRAAM can travel more than 100 miles.

President Donald Trump’s administration has been vocal and adamant about increasing munitions stockpiles for everything from interceptors to air-to-air and air-to-ground missiles.

Separately from the AMRAAM and JATM work, the Air Force is ramping up production under its Family of Affordable Mass Missiles program, which saw a July announcement naming Anduril, CoAspire and Zone Five Technologies as builders of thousands of cruise missiles for air-to-ground engagements.

The companies are expected to produce as many as 5,300 missiles annually starting in 2028 and reach nearly 8,000 missiles a year by 2032.

Not only is the AMRAAM used for air-to-air combat, it is also part of the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System, a midrange air defense system built jointly by Raytheon and Kongsberg Defense & Aerospace.

NASAMS reached operational capability in 1994 and was then deployed by the Royal Norwegian Air Force, according to a 2022 Congressional Research Service report. It can engage 72 targets in both active and passive modes using active-seeker missiles such as the AMRAAM. It has three launchers, each carrying six missiles.

The system uses an AN/MPQ-64 Sentinel Radar, a Fire Distribution Center, and the AMRAAM. The missiles have about a 25-mile range, according to the CRS report.

In 2022, President Joe Biden announced an $820 million aid package to Ukraine, which included funding for two NASAMS. That was followed by six more systems committed later that year and a finalized $1.3 billion contract with Raytheon to build a total of a dozen NASAMs for Ukraine.

Later, the State Department approved an FMS sale of one additional NASAMS to Ukraine in 2023 for $285 million.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said that his nation has more than 10 NASAMS in operation.

In 2024, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported that Japan would begin to co-produce AMRAAMs.

Mitsubishi Heavy Industries is the missile manufacturer under a license agreement. However, as of April 2026, the company was still in discussions “regarding the scope of Japan’s participation in the AIM-120 AMRAAM” program, according to a company release. Separately, the Pacific nation signed a deal in 2023 to acquire 120 AMRAAMs for its own stockpile.

items.title: Fort Bragg opens Rally Point Bistro, bringing campus-style dining to troops
items.author: CPT Thomas McCarty
items.summary: FORT BRAGG, N.C. — Soldiers of all ranks, senior leaders, and community members gathered Tuesday to officially cut the ribbon on the Rally Point Bistro, opening Fort Bragg’s first Campus-Style Dining Venue.
items.body:
FORT BRAGG, N.C. — Soldiers of all ranks, senior leaders, and community members gathered Tuesday to officially cut the ribbon on the Rally Point Bistro, opening Fort Bragg’s first Campus-Style Dining Venue.

Located across from the Soldier Support Center at 41833 Normandy Dr., the venue reimagines traditional military food service by replacing standard cafeteria-style lines with an interactive, college-style dining experience. Managed in partnership with Compass Group USA, Inc., the facility offers extended, continuous operating hours, digital ordering kiosks, locally sourced menus, and performance-focused nutrition aligned with the Army’s Holistic Health and Fitness (H2F) system.

The Fort Bragg opening represents the fourth operational launch under the Army’s initial five-installation CSDV pilot, following successful openings at Fort Hood, Texas; Fort Carson, Colorado; and Fort Drum, New York.

Addressing an audience of distinguished visitors, Gold Star families, Soldiers and Paratroopers, Lt. Gen. Gavin A. Lawrence, deputy commanding general and acting commander of U.S. Army Materiel Command, framed the opening not merely as the debut of a dining facility, but as a cultural shift in how the military fuels its force.

“Today is much more than the opening of a new dining facility,” Lawrence said. “Rally Point Bistro represents change in how we think about the Army food service ecosystem. Campus-style dining venues give Soldiers greater choices, better access, healthier options, and a dining experience designed around how Soldiers live, train, and work.”

Lawrence emphasized that the initiative directly underpins warfighter readiness and soldier quality of life.

“When we get food service right, ladies and gentlemen, the benefits extend well beyond the dining table,” Lawrence added. “Better food and better access help Soldiers perform at their best. It gives them the fuel they need to train, to recover, and to ultimately stay ready. And just as important, a great dining experience brings Soldiers together and strengthens that sense of community that is so important to our Army.”

The name borrows directly from an essential tactical term. In military operations, a rally point is a designated location where units reassemble, regain accountability, reorganize, and prepare to continue the mission. Operating with that same ethos, the bistro provides service members an environment to refuel and reset between demanding training cycles.

Peter Fetherston, chief executive officer of Compass Group’s business and industry sector, highlighted the global food provider's commitment to delivering scale, culinary excellence, and technological reliability for service members.

“Increasingly now, there is evidence that not just physically, but in terms of mental well-being and cognitive performance, food and nutrition is at the heart of it all,” Fetherston said.

Fetherston shared a note left by a Soldier at 42 Bistro at Fort Hood that praised the impact of the CSDV’s on Soldier quality of life.

“In this simple message, I can’t think of a better way to capture and articulate what this is all about,” Fetherston said. “This is about providing excellence in food and hospitality, and an experience to all the people that allow us to enjoy the freedoms that we do. That’s what brings it more meaning. That’s what brings it more purpose. And I cannot stress enough how much we personally are invested in this.”

Inside, the venue offers a diverse culinary lineup ranging from custom grill items and handcrafted deli sandwiches to flatbreads, global street fare, seasonal salad bars, and functional recovery smoothies. Following Tuesday’s grand opening lunch, the facility transitions to full continuous hours: 6:30 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. Monday through Friday, and 8:30 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. on weekends and federal holidays. Unlike traditional dining facilities that shutter between meal services, the doors remain open all day, ensuring Soldiers can obtain food in line with their operational schedules.

For unaccompanied barracks Soldiers on meal cards, daily entitlements convert into a flexible $39 daily “Freedom Dollar” purchasing value at the digital ordering kiosks, while the rest of the installation community—including families, Department of the Army civilians, retirees, and contractors—is welcome to dine and pay à la carte.

Operationally, partnering with commercial culinary contractors to run garrison facilities directly benefits warfighting readiness. By shifting day-to-day cafeteria operations to industry partners, Army culinary specialists (MOS 92G) are freed to focus entirely on their primary wartime mission: honing tactical field-feeding craft, participating in field exercises, and preparing for combat deployments.

Future enhancements for Rally Point Bistro include the phased introduction of phone and app-based remote ordering, with planned deliveries to designated drop zones situated across Fort Bragg.

Closing his remarks, Lawrence reinforced the Army’s enduring obligation to the service members who train and fight out of the home of the airborne and special operations.

“This is more than just being about food—it’s about quality of life, it’s about community, it’s about readiness,” Lawrence said. “To the Soldiers and families of Fort Bragg, I want you to know that you deserve our very best. And today represents another step forward to delivering it.”

More information regarding daily menus, station schedules, and facility updates will be published through the My Army Post App (MAPA) and official installation communication channels.

items.title: Army officer pleads guilty to domestic violence during Fort Bragg court-martial
items.author: Michelle McCaskill
items.summary: Army Maj. Isaac A. Gutierrez, 35, pleaded guilty to domestic violence and communicating a threat during his court-martial Sept. 21 at the Fort Bragg courtroom. Gutierrez, a military intelligence officer assigned to Headquarters and Headquarters Battery, 82nd Airborne Division Artillery, 82nd Airborne Division, was sentenced by the military judge to 17 months in prison.
items.body:
FORT BRAGG, N.C. – Army Maj. Isaac A. Gutierrez, 35, pleaded guilty to domestic violence and communicating a threat during his court-martial Sept. 21 at the Fort Bragg courtroom.

Gutierrez, a military intelligence officer assigned to Headquarters and Headquarters Battery, 82nd Airborne Division Artillery, 82nd Airborne Division, was sentenced by the military judge to 17 months in prison.

While at his Fort Bragg residence on Jan. 24, 2026, Gutierrez confronted his wife who had just returned home from visiting her father out of state. During the argument, which lasted over an hour, he held his wife at gunpoint and threatened to kill her.

A daughter who was upstairs during the altercation became frightened and called her older sister who was visiting a friend down the street. Concerned, the friend’s father called 911 and requested a welfare check.

A team with the Fort Bragg Military police arrived at the scene and apprehended Gutierrez. He was transported to the Fort Bragg Law Enforcement Center, and his chain of command was notified.

Gutierrez is a graduate of the United States Military Academy at West Point and received his Ranger tab after graduation. Several witnesses testified in court to his exceptional military performance.

“Many people wrongfully believe that being a good Soldier is only about performance at work. The accountability for Maj. Gutierrez’s wife and family shows that the Army takes domestic violence seriously, and that no amount of ‘good work’ for the Army excuses violent behavior,” said Maj. Lauren Browning, prosecutor, Second Circuit, Army Office of Special Trial Counsel. “Moreover, this case shows that the Office of Special Trial Counsel holds Soldiers of all ranks responsible for their criminal behavior.”

“Domestic violence is a betrayal of the Army values Soldiers have committed to uphold; it erodes trust, destroys families, and weakens our force,” said Assistant Director Al Diaz, Department of the Army Criminal Investigation Division. “While no sentence can undo the trauma caused to the victims, this outcome sends a clear message that domestic violence has no place in our ranks.”

Gutierrez will serve his prison sentence at the Midwest Joint Regional Confinement Facility at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

This case was investigated by Army CID’s Carolinas Field Office and the Fort Bragg Office of Provost Marshal. It was prosecuted by Browning and Capt. Seneca Tsang, Office of the Staff Judge Advocate, 82nd Airborne Division.

About the Army Office of Special Trial Counsel: The Army Office of Special Trial Counsel is composed of specially trained military lawyers, legal professionals and support staff responsible for the expert prosecution of murder, sexual assault, domestic violence, child abuse, kidnapping and other serious criminal offenses. Headquartered at Fort Belvoir, Va., OSTC has eight regional headquarters that oversee 28 field offices located worldwide, including locations in Europe and Korea. For more information visit http://www.army.mil/ostc.

To Report a Crime: If you would like to report a crime, have information about a crime, or have been the subject or survivor of a crime, you can submit anonymous tips to Army CID at http://www.p3tips.com/armycid.

items.title: ‘Team 15’ welcomes senior enlisted leader
items.author: Laura Levering
items.summary: The 15th Signal Brigade held a change of responsibility ceremony at Signal Theater, Sept. 25, 2026, signaling the transition from Command Sgt. Maj. Nathaniel A. Piper to Command Sgt. Maj. Christopher E. Stadler.
items.body: FORT GORDON, Ga. – The 15th Signal Brigade held a change of responsibility ceremony at Signal Theater, Sept. 25, 2026, signaling the transition from Command Sgt. Maj. Nathaniel A. Piper to Command Sgt. Maj. Christopher E. Stadler. The ceremony was hosted by Col. Benjamin Schneller, 15th Signal Brigade commander. Schneller opened by honoring Piper for his vast contributions, which reached far beyond the brigade. “Our purpose is to ‘forge and project power’ in the cyberspace domain for our Army and our country; more often than not, the man championing this mantra has been Command Sgt. Maj. ‘Tony’ Piper,” said Schneller. “During meetings with the [Cyber Center of Excellence], the five schoolhouses, or external organizations, Command Sgt. Maj. Piper is always the first to highlight the purpose of our Soldiers in enabling cyberspace operations and command and control for the greatest military in the history of the world.” As the brigade’s senior enlisted leader, Piper was responsible for an average daily student load of more than 5,300 trainees, and hundreds of cadre and staff. He took charge of the brigade in November 2024, shortly after Hurricane Helene came through, leaving parts of the region destroyed and without power. Despite the seemingly impossible challenges that followed, Piper remained steadfast – and an inspiration – through it all. “Command Sgt. Maj. Piper looked at ‘Team 15’ and focused on the ways we are alike. He saw things like love of country, service before self, integrity, and pride,” Schneller said. “Command Sgt. Maj. Piper took those similarities and used them to motivate a collection of individuals and inspire our formation … making our Army more connected and more lethal than ever before.” During his remarks, Piper acknowledged that although he was “tested professionally many times,” some of his greatest challenges had nothing to do with the Army. He then opened up about his mental health struggles, personal shortcomings, and journey to sobriety. “The Army values strength – and it should – but somewhere along the way, many of us begin to believe that strength means never admitting we’re struggling; that leaders always have the answer; that rank somehow makes us immune to pain. I’ve learned otherwise,” Piper said. Sharing ways sobriety changed him, Piper emphasized key lessons that he wanted every Soldier to know. “You can be strong and still struggle. You can be successful and still struggle. You can wear stripes on your chest and still struggle. You can be the person everyone else comes to for answers – and still need somebody to answer the phone when you call,” Piper said. Following a list of personal thank-you’s, Piper welcomed Stadler, his successor, to the helm. “You are inheriting an incredible organization and exceptional people,” he told Stadler. “Trust them, challenge them, listen to them, hold them accountable, take care of them, and give them the opportunity to show you what they’re capable of.” Stadler brings more than 22 years of military service to the brigade. His previous assignment was with 551st Signal Battalion where he served as the battalion command sergeant major. Schneller told the seasoned leader that had no doubt the brigade would continue to learn and grow from Stadler’s leadership. “You know the brigade well, and we are very happy and proud to welcome you back to the family in this new role,” Schneller said. “I look forward to building on the great legacy of this organization together.” Stadler said he was incredibly humbled to serve as the brigade’s senior enlisted leader and assured everyone it was a responsibility that he takes with “utmost seriousness.” “Nothing is more critical to our national defense than training, equipping, and preparing our signal, cyber, ordnance, and public affairs Soldiers,” Stadler said. “They are the ones who enable combatant commanders to ruthlessly fight and win our nation’s wars.” The 15th Signal Brigade was constituted as the 15th Signal Service Battalion at Fort Monmouth, New Jersey, in 1940. It was redesignated and relocated to Fort Gordon, Georgia, in 1986, where it has since remained. The brigade consists of: 369th Signal Battalion; 442nd Signal Battalion; 551st Signal Battalion; 401st Cyber Battalion; and Ordnance Training Detachment-Gordon, 73rd Ordnance Battalion.

items.title: Customer service resources to help you with your TRICARE benefit
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: Have you ever had a question about your TRICARE benefit that left you confused or frustrated? There are resources that can help you with your questions or concerns.
items.body:
Have you ever had a question about your TRICARE benefit that left you confused or frustrated? There are resources that can help you with your questions or concerns.

"Every patient’s journey is unique, and our team is here to listen, support, and guide you—no matter where you are or your circumstance,” said U.S. Navy Capt. Gabrielle Crane, chief of the Patient Experience Branch at the Defense Health Agency. “Connecting with us means you are never alone in your care.”

If you need healthcare guidance outside of business hours, you can call the Global Nurse Advice Line . This service lets you connect with a registered nurse by phone, chat, or video. It’s available 24/7 and free for TRICARE beneficiaries to use. Registered nurses are available to answer your questions, assess your symptoms, and give you advice.

To get help with your benefit, start by contacting the right resource. You can resolve many TRICARE concerns by contacting your regional contractor or the DMDC/DEERS Support Office first.

Questions about TRICARE eligibility or updates to a military service record : Contact your Service Personnel Component or the DMDC/DEERS Support Office (800-538-9552).

Questions about enrollment, claims, provider networks, or referrals : Contact your regional contractor first. Do you disagree with a claim decision? You can file an appeal with the regional contractor. Do you have a complaint about the kind of care you received? You can file a grievance with the regional contractor.

Do you disagree with a claim decision? You can file an appeal with the regional contractor.

Do you have a complaint about the kind of care you received? You can file a grievance with the regional contractor.

Additionally, military hospitals and clinics have staff who can help. These staff can assist you after you work with the regional contractor or DMDC. Each hospital has a customer service team that includes three roles:

Beneficiary Counseling and Assistance Coordinators

Debt Collection Assistance Officers

You don’t have to be a patient at a military hospital or clinic to get help from BCACs or from DCAOs. Contact the customer service team closest to where you live . The DHA created these customer service roles to help you wherever you are. Keep reading to learn when to contact a customer service representative and how to find one.

Healthcare can be complex, but you shouldn’t feel like you're facing it alone. Every military hospital and clinic has a patient advocate, and many also have patient advocates at the unit or section level who help with specific areas of care. Whether you’re an active duty service member, retiree, or family member, a patient advocate is available to address your concerns. They’re trusted resources who can help you with your care, understand your rights, and improve your experience.

Patient advocates listen carefully, investigate, and work with staff to resolve concerns fairly and quickly. They act as mediators to help build understanding between you and your care team. Patient advocates explain policies and your rights in plain language. Their role is to make sure you feel support and respect.

If you’d like to compliment a staff member, your patient advocate will make sure to give your appreciation to the right leaders. Patient advocates also find trends in patient feedback and promote improvements.

DHA uses a Patient Advocate Assistance Reporting Tool across all military hospitals and clinics. This system helps patient advocates track and work through all patient concerns. This system provides leadership at every level with critical transparency. It helps them identify trends and make data-driven improvements to the overall patient experience.

BCACs help you understand how your TRICARE plan works. They can answer TRICARE-related questions and work with the regional contractors to make sure your care follows TRICARE policy. BCACs can address TRICARE-related questions including:

Referrals and pre-authorizations

Getting healthcare services outside the military hospital or clinic

A BCAC can help you understand messages you see in your Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System record. They can also guide you on how to follow up with your sponsor’s Service Personnel Component. BCACs don’t determine or fix TRICARE eligibility—but they can help you understand the process.

DCAOs help resolve debt collections due to late or unpaid TRICARE claims. The debt must be in collections or listed on your credit report before a DCAO can work with you.

A DCAO isn’t a legal representative. But they can ask the collection agency to hold on their efforts so the government can research the debt and find out who is responsible for paying the bill.

How to find help

Each military hospital or clinic has contact information for the patient advocate, BCAC, and DCAO. If you want to visit in person, you can ask the hospital staff for their office location. You can also find contact information for all three roles using the Customer Service Community Directory . Or, check out the Customer Service page on your military hospital or clinic’s website .

Three roles, one mission

Patient advocates, BCACs, and DCAOs each bring unique experience to a shared mission. Together, they form a unified resource to help you in your healthcare journey. Whether you need answers about TRICARE benefits, guidance on a claim, or advocacy for your overall healthcare experience, the customer service community is here for you.

Patient advocates champion your voice, ensuring that your concerns are heard, and your rights are protected. BCACs simplify TRICARE, translating complex policies into clear guidance so you can access your benefits with confidence. DCAOs protect your financial peace of mind, helping when billing disputes or collections overwhelm you.

Knowing there are people to help when you have concerns with your healthcare is important. The next time you have questions your regional contractor can’t answer, contact a member of the customer service team at your closest military hospital or clinic.

items.title: Every Airman plays a part in cyber defense
items.author: Jessica Kendziorek
items.summary: Cybersecurity begins with individual choices; from recognizing suspicious emails to protecting personal information and reporting potential threats quickly. As computers remain central to daily operations, every Airman has a role in maintaining a secure and ready force. Communications, cyber, intelligence-support, and security personnel support that effort by helping members identify common online threats and apply safe practices both on and off duty.
items.body:
Cybersecurity begins with individual choices; from recognizing suspicious emails to protecting personal information and reporting potential threats quickly.

As computers remain central to daily operations, every Airman has a role in maintaining a secure and ready force. Communications, cyber, intelligence-support, and security personnel support that effort by helping members identify common online threats and apply safe practices both on and off duty.

“Cybersecurity is not limited to the people who work in communications or cyber units,” said Master Sgt. Michael Sielke-Meade, the Senior Enlisted Leader for the 403rd Communications Flight. “Every Airman who uses a government device, accesses an account, or receives an email is part of the defensive team.”

The Air Force network is under constant attack 24/7. While major network operations squadrons and cyber operations squadrons actively defend and patch the network, individual passive defense is a critical line of security.

Sielke-Meade said that this passive defense can feel tedious at times, but maintaining updates, managing application lists, and ensuring only approved software is run on the network plays a vital part.

“Even if it may not feel like it, every single member has a role to play in keeping the network secure,” he said.

Phishing remains one of the most common methods malicious actors use to gain access to information and systems by exploiting the human factor. These messages are designed to look as official and familiar as possible to trick people into clicking links, letting an attacker onto the network, or capturing credentials, passwords, and personal identification numbers.

Airmen should pause before responding to unexpected messages, verify the sender through an established contact method, and avoid entering credentials or personal information through unverified links.

“Attackers often rely on urgency, curiosity, or familiarity to get someone to act before they think,” said Sielke-Meade. “Taking a few seconds to verify an email or report something suspicious can prevent a much larger issue.”

Protecting personally identifiable information and maintaining system updates also remain critical parts of digital readiness. To keep NIPRNet secure, Airmen should run Windows updates, automated remediation, Office 365 updates, and group policy updates at least two to three times weekly. Additionally, performing a full computer restart at least once every 24 hours in conjunction with these updates keeps the network safe and running smoothly.

Sielke-Meade said that if an Airman receives a suspected phishing message, they should not forward it. Instead, they should do nothing with it and report it directly to their Unit Security Manager, the 403rd Communications Flight, or to the 81st Communications Squadron, where security personnel will block the sender or direct the user to delete the message.

In cases where an Airman notices active, unusual activity and suspects their computer is compromised, he reminds them to take immediate action.

He said that the first step is to disconnect the computer from the network cable. Airmen must not log off or shutdown the machine; instead, they should bring the computer straight to the 403rd Communications Flight, or the 81st Communications Squadron if they are unavailable, so cyber personnel can perform an intake, evaluate the system, and remediate the issue.

“Good cyber hygiene protects the individual, but it also protects teammates and the mission,” Sielke-Meade said. “A secure force is a more resilient force.”

By remaining alert, safeguarding information, running routine updates, and promptly reporting concerns, Airmen help preserve the systems and networks that enable the Air Force Reserve mission.

items.title: The Story of Strontium-90 at Hunter's Point Naval Shipyard
items.author: Kathleen Roberts
items.summary: This video discusses the Navy’s collaborative process with federal and state regulatory agencies to identify the best Strontium (Sr)-90 analytical method to use for testing soil samples from the former Hunters Point Naval Shipyard. Beginning in 2021, Navy chemists observed inconsistent results when testing Parcel G soil samples for Sr-90 using the initial standard laboratory method, EPA Method 905
items.body: This video discusses the Navy’s collaborative process with federal and state regulatory agencies to identify the best Strontium (Sr)-90 analytical method to use for testing soil samples from the former Hunters Point Naval Shipyard. Beginning in 2021, Navy chemists observed inconsistent results when testing Parcel G soil samples for Sr-90 using the initial standard laboratory method, EPA Method 905. This method failed to produce consistent results upon reanalysis of the same sample. Due to concerns about accuracy, the Navy collaborated with the United States Environmental Protection Agency, California Department of Toxic Substances Control, and California Department of Public Health to identify an alternate method to detect Sr-90 at very low levels with the precision required for decision-making. The Eichrom Method for Total Beta Strontium (TBS) analyzes for all Sr in in soil samples. It has been shown to be reliable and accurate for the low Sr-90 concentration level for the Parcel G Sr-90 remedial goal set at 0.331 pCi/g. This goal is more than 10 times lower than the typical regulatory standard and ensures protectiveness of human health and the environment. Using the validated and verified Eichrom Method for TBS, the Navy is able to accurately and reliably detect low levels of Sr-90 in soil samples. By following this standard, the Navy ensures that the cleanup at HPNS goes beyond regulatory requirements, offering extra protection to human health and the environment.

items.title: National Foster Alliance brings Pet adoption opportunities to Fort Buchanan
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: National Foster Alliance volunteers connected with military families, service members and civilian employees Aug. 29-30 at Fort Buchanan, the Army’s home in the Caribbean, during a two-day outreach event promoting pet adoption, foster care and responsible animal welfare while addressing Puerto Rico’s widespread stray and abandoned animal problem.
items.body:
FORT BUCHANAN, Puerto Rico — National Foster Alliance volunteers connected with military families, service members and civilian employees Aug. 29-30 at Fort Buchanan, the Army’s home in the Caribbean, during a two-day outreach event promoting pet adoption, foster care and responsible animal welfare while addressing Puerto Rico’s widespread stray and abandoned animal problem.

The event highlighted Fort Buchanan’s connection to the broader Puerto Rico community. Stray and abandoned dogs remain a concern across the island, and the outreach gave members of the Fort Buchanan community an opportunity to support adoption, fostering and responsible pet ownership.

The event also marked the beginning of a partnership National Foster Alliance hopes to continue with Fort Buchanan, according to Shirley Prado, the organization’s foster program coordinator.

“The experience was very positive,” Prado said. “The questions, the genuine interest, the support, the interactions … truly surprised us.”

Throughout the event, volunteers introduced community members to National Foster Alliance programs, explained adoption and fostering processes and answered questions about caring for rescued animals.

The organization also brought adoptable pets to the installation as part of Telemundo’s Clear the Shelters 2026 campaign, allowing community members to meet animals searching for permanent homes.

The outreach produced an immediate result when one dog found a new home after the adopter completed the organization’s required application and interview process.

The event also generated interest in fostering. A couple applied to become foster caregivers and later welcomed a dog into their home while it completed veterinary care.

National Foster Alliance’s foster program provides temporary homes for rescued animals, pets recovering from veterinary treatment and animals awaiting adoption. Foster families provide safe environments while animals prepare for permanent placement.

Prado said the Fort Buchanan community’s diversity and willingness to participate demonstrated the partnership’s potential.

“Everyone at the military installation showed a level of openness and warmth that truly surprised us,” Prado said. “They wanted to learn more, collaborate, and participate in future activities. For us, it was confirmation that this type of collaboration has a huge impact.”

National Foster Alliance is scheduled to return to Fort Buchanan Nov. 14-15 for another outreach event featuring adoptable pets, informational activities and its “Cada Mascota Cuenta,” or “Every Pet Counts,” campaign.

The campaign teaches children compassion, responsibility and respect for animals while helping families understand the commitment involved in caring for a pet.

The upcoming event will provide another opportunity for the Fort Buchanan military community to learn about fostering, meet adoptable animals and support efforts to place rescued pets in safe, permanent homes.

The continuing partnership reflects Fort Buchanan’s role in the Puerto Rico community by giving Soldiers, families and civilian employees opportunities to support organizations addressing challenges across the island. Fort Buchanan supports approximately 15,000 military personnel, including active-duty Soldiers, Army Reserve, Puerto Rico National Guard, Marine Corps Reserve and Navy Reserve members. The installation’s mission is to enable readiness and facilitate the deployment of forces anytime, anywhere.
